item.title: Casing The HPC And AI-Sci Market With Hyperion Research
item.description:
When you go to the Super Computing conference in America or the International Super Computing conference in Europe, one of the hardest things to do is get up early on a Tuesday morning and hustle on over to the IDC and now Hyperion Research breakfast to get a good greasy breakfast and some strong coffee. But you do it so you can be alert for an update on the state of the HPC and now AI for Science markets, and because this breakfast usually follows a very social evening on Monday, if you catch my drift.

If you can make it to that breakfast, you will make it through the week.

I was not able to attend ISC26 or SC26 this year for medical reasons, but I did get my hands on the presentation put together by Earl Joseph, Bob Sorensen, and Mark Nossokoff for the SC26 breakfast, which gives us a sense of how the first half of 2026 turned out in HPC and AI-Sci Land and also gave out forecasts for spending for on premises gear and for capacity on the clouds aimed at simulation, modeling, and AI for science workloads.

The revenues in the chart above for on premises HPC and AI-Sci systems are in millions of dollars, and as you can see, the spending from January through June was up 19.9 percent to $16.48 billion. (It would be helpful to put the dollar signs in the chart so people know what the numerical units are for each category.) While revenue was up smartly, worldwide unit shipments of on premises HPC and AI-Sci systems only increased by 4.4 percent compared to the first half of 2025. The gap between the two come from having more nodes per system, slightly higher numbers of CPUs per system, and price increases for CPUs, GPUs, DRAM, and flash.

Frankly, we are surprised the increased pricing for components is not more of the gap, and that might be an expression that HPC centers are being more conservative and hanging back one or two generations on CPUs and GPUs so they can get a lower capital outlay than it would take to buy a current system. We do see a lot of Grace-Hopper systems or Intel Xeon-Hopper systems being added in the current Top500 supercomputer rankings and for the prior couple of lists, even though Grace-Blackwell systems have been available for two years now. More current GPUs are too scarce and too expensive for most HPC centers.

While Hewlett Packard Enterprise has been the leading in HPC and AI-Sci on premises installs for many years, since acquiring SGI and Cray, in the first half of 2026 Dell has emerged as the revenue leader.

Again, this table is in dollars, not unit shipments. Dell’s HPC and AI-Sci system sales were up 67.7 percent in the first half of 2026 to $3.93 billion, while HPE only grew its on premises technical computing revenues by 1.1 percent to $3.44 billion. It is hard to say if this is driven by allocations of GPUs by Nvidia or AMD – Dell has been getting preferential treatment in the past two years from Nvidia for AI systems in general. (It was a billionaire thing between Michael Dell and Jensen Huang, the latter of which no longer runs Nvidia.) It would be interesting to see how many aggregate FP64 flops HPE and Dell sold against those revenues. For all we know, HPE is still winning in the flops race against Dell in the HPC and AI-Sci space.

The revenues per vendor drop off pretty fast below Dell and HPE, as you can see, with dozens of system builders – both OEMs and ODMs – accounting for $9.12 billion in sales for the first half of 2026, up 13.8 percent compared to 19.9 percent for the market at large. Dell’s growth and its size are lifting the class average bigtime. It is too early to tell if Dell will retain its position for the second half of 2026, and we won’t know that until the ISC27 Hyperion Research breakfast next year in Hamburg next June.

It could turn out that HPE is selling a lot more CPU-only machines for traditional HPC ModSim workloads, and Dell is getting more GPU allocations and is selling more machines with accelerators – and not just for GenAI workloads.

We don’t have any numbers for 2026 as yet, which is still not finished, but Joseph flashed up this interesting chart showing how the installed base of GPUs in the HPC and AI-Sci market have changed between 2017 and 2025:

To my eyes, we keep going at the same pace as between 2024 and 2025 this year, and that means 2026 should end with about 1.2 million GPU accelerators installed worldwide in HPC and AI-Sci systems.

This may sound like a lot, but you always need a compared-to-what context to put things into perspective. Doing some back of the envelope math, There is an installed base of somewhere between 18 million and 20 million GPUs – and that means everything that has shipped in the past six or seven years that is still in the field because no one is unplugging a GPU that isn’t reused somewhere immediately. There is probably another 13 million to 17 million custom AI XPUs in the fleet as well, with Google having the lion’s share with its TPUs (somewhere between 9 million and 11 million). Amazon might have 3 million Trainiums and maybe 1 million to 2 million Inferentia chips. Microsoft and Meta Platforms have hundreds of thousands of Maia and MTIA accelerators, respectively. The Chinese custom XPUs are noise in this data, and China hates that this is true.  So that 1.2 million GPUs for HPC and AI-Sci represents somewhere between 3 percent and 4 percent of the total worldwide fleet of 31 million to 37 million GPUs and XPUs that are up and running in the world. (The lower percent is against the higher GPU and XPU installed base, obviously.)

For further perspective, HPC and AI-Sci spending is on the order of several tens of billions per year, including power and datacenter construction, while AI proper with training and inference together is between two and three orders of magnitude larger.

The AI tail that used to be on the HPC dog a decade and a half ago has been cloned and is now dozens of sled teams of dogs that are larger in size than the original parent dog. Which has got to be very weird for the HPC crowd that has spent decades at the bleeding edge of systems architecture and high performance.

Now, I have a DGX Spark baby supercomputer – and that is what it is – under my desk, which I will be using for some AI model experimentation. If I could send this baby supercomputer back in time to 1979 and land it on Seymour Cray’s desk, he would have wept with joy.

We truly do live in the future. . . .

Speaking of the future, let’s look at some Hyperion Research forecasts, starting with the forecast for on premises HPC and AI-Sci servers:

Basically, this market will triple in a decade ending in 2030, which is decent growth even if it is not exponential like the GenAI boom has been for the past four years. As you can see, the bulk of the sales of on premises HPC and AI-Sci gear is for larger-scale supercomputers, but divisional, departmental, and workgroup systems are still selling at roughly the same proportion today as they were five years ago and moreover are expected to sell at about the same rate four years from now as the decade comes to a close.

Joseph says that the broader HPC and AI-Sci market, including storage, middleware, applications, services, and cloud compute, networking, and storage capacity, will exceed $100 billion in 2030 against $54 billion in on premises system sales.

Of course, HPC centers rent clusters as well as buying them, and you have to count that, too:

As you might expect, there is more spending on the cloud for HPC and AI-Sci applications in North America than in the EMEA and Asia/Pacific regions even though the European and Asia economies as two groups are formidable economic regions in their own right.

Over the forecast period from 2022 through 2030, spending on cloud capacity for HPC and AI-Sci applications will grow by nearly 5X by 2030 to around $30 billion. (Why this forecast didn’t have 2021 as the baseline year like the on premises chart did is unclear.)

Just to make it simple and readily apparent, Hyperion Research put the on premises acquisitions and cloud rental spending for infrastructure for HPC and AI-Sci workloads into a single chart:

Back in 2022, the combined infrastructure spending was just north of $40 billion, and it will grow by 3.4X or so to $135 billion in 2030.

It may look like cloud spending is a lot lower, but you have to remember that the on premises spending is for five years. If you add up five years of cloud spending and compare it to the on premises spending for a particular year, the amount of money being spent for a given number of compute-hours over time is a lot closer than it looks. On premises spending is probably a little larger than cloud spending when looked at this way. And remember: Both on premises revenues and cloud rentals include price increases driven by higher component costs that are definitely being passed on to the end user customers.

The issue is whether the amount of HPC and AI-Sci work is cheaper to be done on premises than on the cloud, and there are a lot of ways to argue about that. What is clear is that many HPC centers are doing both and are expected to continue in this practice.

item.title: Nvidia Breaks Revenue And Profit Records, And Will Keep Doing It
item.description:
Nvidia’s first chairman of the board, Harvey Jones, who was hired in November 1993 to join the Nvidia board seven months after the company was co-founded by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem, wasted no time to quash any thought on the call with Wall Street analysts going over Nvidia's third quarter fiscal 2027 financial results concerning chatter about Huang returning to the chief executive officer position at Nvidia.

And I quote:

“Nvidia is an exceptionally strong company. Its strength comes from its extraordinary people, groundbreaking technology and exemplary track record of execution. Our financial performance speaks for itself.”

“On November 12, our Board of Directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO. The board appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia’s longtime and well-respected CFO, as interim CEO. In addition, the Board announced it was initiating a search for a permanent chief executive, and we have since retained Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search.”

While this was an unexpected transition, the Board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders.”

So, that’s that. Unless shareholders vote to throw out the current board of directors and vote in a board that tries to reinstate Huang. Which seems unlikely.

Nvidia is riding so high and its employees know full well how to ramp up “Vera-Rubin” systems, which they are doing now, as well as get the “Vera-Rubin Ultra” follow-on systems out the door next year and the “Feynman” GPUs and what we presume will be a new and accompanying CPU architecture out the door in 2028. We said as much on November 12 in The Nvidia Machine Is Self-Sustaining – And Was Already Facing A Tougher Future , the day Huang resigned.

Kress finished the call with Wall Street, where she walked through the numbers and answered question along with Jones, in this direct fashion: “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us and employees are committed. We've got this.”

So, there you have it.

With that, let’s take a look at the Nvidia third quarter financial results and the upwardly revised forecast for fiscal 2028.

In the quarter ended in October, Nvidia brought in a record-setting $115.8 billion in revenues, a little more than double the sales it had across all of its products a year ago. Net income was 56.4 percent of revenue, which works out to an astounding $65.3 billion, which also more than doubled year on year.

As I have said before: Just amazing .

Nvidia returned $28 billion back to shareholders during the quarter, with $22 billion in share buybacks on Wall Street and another $6 billion in dividends. Nvidia currently has $227 billion in authorization for share buybacks and just added another $150 billion as the third quarter came to a close. That $337 billion is expected to be spent on buybacks before the end of fiscal 2028. Which is just an astounding number. It took IBM decades to blow that much dough on share buybacks to engineer its earnings per share – the growth of which was how IBM rewarded Wall Street and its executive ranks with stock grants and other bonuses.

Nvidia ended Q3 F2027 with $97.7 billion in cash and investments, up 61.3 percent year on year.

For the past several years, Nvidia has kept the books with two different divisions: Compute & Networking is one and Graphics is the other.

In the third quarter, Compute & Networking, which has a small portion of sales outside of the datacenter, accounted for just a hair under $106 billion, up 2.1X year on year and up 20 percent sequentially from Q2 F2027. The Graphics group, which sells graphics cards for PCs, laptops, gamers, and scientific and professional workstations, brought in a modest and yet record-breaking $9.85 billion in sales, up 61.5 percent year on year.

Beginning this year, with the datacenter business just utterly dwarfing its workstation, automotive, gaming, visualization, and OEM/IP divisions, Nvidia reclassified itself into different divisions, and this quarter the numbers were restated as a neocloud became a cloud as its business model changed and Nvidia back cast revised data as this company was moved from he Datacenter Hyperscale division to the Datacenter AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise division.

The Datacenter Hyperscale division is what I call the hyperscalers (those that run vast consumer-facing applications) and the cloud builders (those who sell infrastructure and software as services). The AI model builders OpenAI and Anthropic are on their way to be hyperscalers as well, with the way they are spending on IT infrastructure to support their enormous AI training and inference workloads. In the third quarter, these customers spent $60.14 billion on Nvidia wares, up 71.1 percent year on year and up 23.5 percent sequentially.

The Datacenter AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise division – often abbreviated ACIE by Nvidia employees – covers sales of Nvidia hardware to sovereign clouds, neoclouds, industrial companies, and enterprises. Governments and academic institutions are also in this division, although the name does not suggest this. The ACIE division had $47.47 billion in sales, up nearly 3X year on year and it probably will not be long before these ACIE customers, who are focused on inference, will do more spending than the hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders that have made Nvidia filthy rich.

Kress said on the call that Nvidia’s networking business brought in more than $21 billion in sales, and I have estimated how this break downs across the InfiniBand, Ethernet/Other product lines – other being NVSwitch memory fabrics. I estimate that InfiniBand switches, cables, and optics raked in $9.32 billion in sales, up 2.2X year on year, while Ethernet/Other brought in $11.97 billion, up more than 3X year on year. If you pushed me for a further breakdown for networking, I would estimate that Ethernet switching (which again includes cables and optics in addition to switching) drove $6.64 billion in sales, up 2.6X year on year, while NVSwitch drove $5.43 billion in revenues, up 3.8X year on year.

Datacenter compute, which means both CPUs and GPUs, accounted for $86.32 billion in sales in Q3 F2027, and more than doubled compared to Q2 F2026.

Looking ahead, Kress said that Nvidia was expecting $130 billion in sales, give or take 3 percent, in Q4 F2027, driven by the strong Vera-Rubin platform ramp, and that the company was raising its guidance for F2028, saying it would grow by 75 percent compared to F2027. Only a few quarters ago, Wall Street was expecting F2028 to grow maybe 45 percent, and last quarter Nvidia said it expected 70 percent growth in F2028. The demand is strong for Nvidia’s products, and the revenue increase is really about getting more supply that it can put into the field.

Kress also said on the call that the “cloud industry backlog” was now $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion only three months ago. I presume this means hyperscalers plus neoclouds and sovereign clouds, minus industrial, enterprise, government, and academic customers.

item.title: IBM Links Two Nighthawk r3 Chips To Make A 1,040-Qubit Quantum System
item.description:
Big Blue has been on a tear for the past couple of years detailing the strides it’s making towards meeting its ambitious goal of launching a fault-tolerant quantum computer in 2029, highlighting progress in a range of areas, from error correction and quantum advantage to more tightly tying together quantum and classical HPC computing.

A year ago this month, IBM announced Nighthawk (below), a follow-on to its Heron quantum processor that includes 120 qubits and its square-lattice architecture, a shift in topology away from its earlier heavy-hex technology that brings greater qubit connectivity, crosstalk management, and circuit depth performance. In September, IBM unveiled Nighthawk r2, another 120-qubit QPU that comes with a new reset system that pushes throughput up to more than 100,000 circuits per second.

In the meantime, research papers have outlined three demonstrations of quantum advantage run on IBM’s Heron quantum chips and the unveiling of a modular and scalable cryogenic cooling system that will be critical to its plans for the fault-tolerant Starling system in 2029 and another example of the company’s modular approach to quantum infrastructure.

The also were announcements about achievements made with partners, including AMD and Oak Ridge National Laboratory in quantum-classical computing error correction and the RIKEN Institute in Japan and the Cleveland Clinic about the work that can be done now with hybrid quantum and classical computing in scientific research .

This week, at the IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 in Chicago, the company outlined advancements in speed and quality the Nighthawk r2 QPUs are making and plans to run out Nighthawk r3, its next-generation quantum chip, in 2027. The company also plans to release a device that will use long-range couplers (l-couplers) to join together two Nighthawk r3 processors into a single system.

IBM executives said that when talking about quantum workloads, speed is just as important as scale and quality, noting that more applications are requiring circuits that can execute thousands of operations on 100 qubits or more to generation millions to billions of samples. Quantum systems will need to see jumps in speed to ensure such applications can be run fast enough and at acceptable costs.

The design for Nighthawk r2 is already making strides in that direction, according to Oliver Dial, IBM Fellow and the vendor’s senior vice president of quantum systems. As with the first Nighthawk iteration, r2 includes 120 qubits, but it also comes with on-chip qubit reset, Dial told journalists during a briefing before the event.

“This is an extra physical qubit that we glued on the chip for each programmable qubit that lets us quickly remove the energy from one of our programmable qubits, returning it to the ground state,” he said. “That capability lets our users run circuits on this chip faster than was ever before possible. In fact, in the first three weeks that this device was available, our users ran 8 billion circuits on it.”

Since September, more than 34 billion circuits have run on Nighthawk r2, and IBM has run 7,500 gates on the chip, 19 times faster than it would have taken for Nighthawk r1 due to the reset capability.

Nighthawk r3 will scale to more 520 qubits and support 10,000 quantum operations and, while retaining the square-lattice connectivity, will include 10 chip-to-chip l-coupler interconnects that can be used for larger quantum systems. Connecting two Nighthawk r3 processors will create a 1,040-qubit system that can run larger and more complex computations.

Nighthawk r3 will be manufactured at the Anderon 300-millimeter quantum superconducting wafer foundry in Albany, New York. (Below) Anderon is an IBM subsidiary that expanded its operations after the US Commerce Department in May contributed $1 billion through the federal CHIPS Act. IBM contributed a $1 billion investment of its own. As a side note, Global Foundries also received $375 million from the Commerce Department to develop a quantum foundry.

The l-couplers are key to performance and scalability improvements, Dial said. IBM connected Nighthawk r1 processors using four l-couplers and reaching 99.3 percent quantum state transfer fidelity, closing in on the company’s goal of 99.9 percent.

“And cooling down right now in Poughkeepsie, New York [home of IBM’s Quantum Data Center] is a first, joining two processors in two different refrigerators with four l-couplers, only this time is Nighthawk r2s,” Dial said. “We think that this progress shows that we are well advanced on our path towards building Starling.”

Starling is expected to be the fault-tolerant system that arrives in 2029, with 200 logical qubits capable of running 100 million quantum operations. A key for IBM with Starling is the planned use of bivariate bicycle codes, a class of quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) error correction codes that reduce the number of physical qubits needed to make up logical qubits and the quantum information they hold.

Starling’s successor, Blue Jay, will come in 2033 or later.

“A lot of the technologies that we're premiering in Nighthawk are also going to help us build Starling,” he said. “Our path to large-scale fault tolerance is the only practical approach to fault tolerance out there. That's because it's built on a universal Pauli-based computation architecture that uses an error-correcting code that’s over 10x more efficient than alternatives [like surface codes]. It's built on a modular platform, which lets us build modules that are the same size and complexity as what we're already capable of building today and join them together to build this enormous platform.”

Dial added: “It's that modularity and the efficiency of this design that's really key to the practicality. There are several key technologies that we need to demonstrate in order to bring this architecture to reality. This includes device physics for higher connectivity – c-couplers – packaging for more signals, decoders, the ability to detect and correct a computation for the presence of errors, modular QPUs with l-couplers, as mentioned before for Nighthawk R3, a modular cryogenic system, and modular control electronics.”

Asked what other milestones need to be reached for starling, Dial pointed to “bigger, better devices,” “more wiring,” the capability to demonstrate the modular cryogenic cooling system at a scale about three times more than what they can do today, and the ability to run decoding in real time.

IBM also continues to push the tighter alignment of quantum systems with classical computers. The latest step introduced at the event this week is IBM bringing classical HPC computing and quantum into a single managed environment on IBM’s Quantum Platform, which will allow organizations to integrate quantum workflows with a classical compute, ranging from laptops to supercomputers, or with classical resources now available on the platform.

It dovetails with IBM’s announcement this month of a co-design platform for error correction that brought together Big Blue’s Nighthawk r2 and Oak Ridge’s Umbra supercomputer – powered by AMD Epyc datacenter chips and Instinct GPUs – in the same datacenter in Poughkeepsie, New York.

The managed offering “allows you to provision for a class of compute, ranging in different sizes of compute, from CPU-based all the way up to GPU-based, and have it in the same environment in which you are running your quantum computer execution,” said Jerry Chow, IBM Fellow and chief technology officer of quantum-centric supercomputing. “You can have persistence across the jobs that you want to run, as well as a simple way to pay for both the classical and quantum resources in one place.”

item.title: Quantinuum Aligns Software Development For Quantum Hardware Generations
item.description:
A week rarely goes by without news of significant advancements in the ongoing development of quantum computing, whether it is around error correction and fault tolerance , architectures and infrastructure, post-quantum cryptography, or tighter integrations between quantum and classical HPC systems.

None of this is lost on enterprises, which are increasingly investigating how they can use the technology now and really benefit from it when more practical, scalable, and fault-tolerant systems begin to emerge in force in the coming years. According to analysts with global consultancy McKinsey & Co, more than 300 organizations across the global are working with quantum computing providers, and even more are experimenting with the technology.

“Many business leaders now accept that quantum technology is coming sooner than they first expected, and they’re taking steps today to capture a competitive advantage,” they wrote in a report last month . “Faced with quantum technology’s rapid pace of development and the scale of its implications, leaders are now forced to reconsider their action plans. ... Quantum technology companies are hitting milestones more quickly than they initially predicted, and many have ambitious road maps that put the expected arrival of fault-tolerant quantum computing within the next few years.”

Included in the ambitious roadmaps for many such vendors is the development of full-stack quantum offerings, moving beyond creating qubits and the hardware that goes around them to including software, developer tools, capabilities for hybrid quantum-classical and cloud environments, AI integrations, and APIs for optimization.

It was a driving force behind Intel’s bid to buy quantum software maker Classiq for $2.3 billion . In announcing the deal late last month, Intel chief technology officer Pushkar Ranade explained that Intel had spent a decade building its quantum chips and SDK and running its quantum operation as something akin to a science project. Having Classiq in the fold “moves our quantum computing group from just a research-and-development focus to an actual quantum computing business,” Ranade said.

The list of quantum companies building out full-stack capabilities includes IBM , D-Wave , Rigetti, and IonQ , among others. Quantinuum is another one, with the vendor matching its generations of quantum systems and as-a-service offerings (below) with advances in software – such as its InQuanto and Quantum Origin applications – and developer tools, from its Nexus developer platform two years ago to the toolkit for Guppy, its Python-based programming language.

The growing attention by vendors on quantum software and developer tools “tells us the field is becoming more focused on what it takes to make quantum computing useful,” Josh Savory, senior director of offering management for Quantinuum, tells The Next Platform . “Qubit count matters, but customers ultimately need accurate answers at the speed their applications require. That takes highly accurate hardware, scalable error correction, software, and integration with classical computing. Customers should start preparing now. Building application expertise, testing error-corrected programs, and integrating quantum computation into classical workflows all take time.”

The five-year-old company closely co-designs the hardware, error correction, and compilers with the developer tools, which Savory says lets developers take advantage of advances in the underlying hardware as quickly as possible.

To that end, Quantinuum – which was formed in 2021 in the merger of Honeywell’s quantum division and quantum software company Cambridge Quantum Computing – earlier this month unveiled a new roadmap for its Nexus platform (below), outlining new capabilities with the upcoming next-generation hardware leading up to Apollo, the vendor’s first fault-tolerant system scheduled for 2029.

The company last year launched Helios (below), it’s third-generation trapped-ion quantum system that includes 98 qubits and which in October reached 99.9995 percent accuracy – five errors in a million operations – which company executives said was within the target range for Apollo. Along with Helios, Quantinuum includes such capabilities in Nexus as customized error suppression to optimize code performance, prebuilt primitives and logical qubits with proprietary codes, and the InQuanto quantum chemistry platform.

More Nexus advancements are scheduled for next year, when the vendor runs out its Sol system, and then again with Apollo two years after that.

Savoy points to Guppy FT – a fault-tolerant programming framework and extension of the Guppy language – as an example of how Quantinuum connects software development with the company’s architecture, allowing developers to focus on algorithms while specialists improve how the algorithms are protected and executed. The vendor released Guppy FT and Guppy Algorithms – an open-source library of reusable building blocks and algorithmic primitives – in September.

“The Nexus roadmap extends that connection across hardware generations,” he says. “We want the applications, workflows, and expertise customers build today to become more valuable as the systems advance. Our full stack strategy also focuses on integrating our tools across the broader ecosystem. Nexus supports tools developers already use, including [Nvidia’s] CUDA-Q and Q# [open source language created by Microsoft], and is designed to fit into cloud, on-premises, and in high-performance computing environments. The aim is to give developers an integrated path while supporting the broader ecosystem.”

Pacing the development of the software and development tools with the hardware advancements will be important as more organizations begin growing their use of quantum computing. Savoy says that 215 companies are building on Nexus, with job submissions increasing 10x in the 12 months through August when compared with the previous 12 months.

The release of the Nexus roadmap comes amid a number of other efforts by Quantinuum. Along with the error-corrections results from Helios in October, the vendor earlier this month announced it had upgraded the Reimei quantum computer housed at the RIKEN institute in Japan from its 20-qubit H1 system to a 56-qubit H2 computer.

The H2 system will allow RIKEN scientists to combine quantum computing, supercomputing, and AI. In a separate announcement, Quantinuum, RIKEN, and Japanese multinational conglomerate SoftBank also explore how quantum systems can be directly connected to AI datacenters in Japan.

Quantinuum in the third quarter also reported $9.1 million in revenue, a 233 percent year-over-year increase from $2.7 million and pushed its full-year revenue outlook from $31 million to $34 million. Savoy says its co-development efforts will help.

“The important distinction is between developing supported error-corrected applications today and delivering universal fault tolerance at scale,” he says. “We are enabling the former while working toward the latter. Our hardware, software, and commercial ecosystem are parts of one strategy: give customers a reason to build with Quantinuum today and a path to carry that investment into the fault-tolerant era.”

item.title: Supercomputer Installs Take A Dive In The Second Half Of 2026
item.description:
Given that compute engines and networks are constantly being updated and that HPC centers the world over have their own budget and upgrade cycles, there has been a fairly constant level of new machines being installed at any given time.

This has always been reflected in the Top500 supercomputer rankings that come out twice a year – first in June with the International Supercomputing (ISC) event in Europe and then again in November with the Super Computing (SC) event held in the United States. But on the November 2026 Top 500 list, new machine installations – and to be precise, new machines that have been tested using the High Performance LINPACK (HPL) benchmark test to gauge their relative performance – stalled and the number of machines is about half what we normally expect.

This is not a good sign, and it might show perhaps how priorities are shifting to renting capacity on clouds instead of trying to acquire a new machine every four or five years and building a datacenter to support ever-hotter and ever-more-expensive HPC systems.

But don’t freak out just yet. It could also just be that companies were not ready to test iron that is being installed now or early in 2027 as Nvidia rolls out its “Rubin” GR200 GPUs and “Vera” CV100 CPUs or AMD rolls out its “Altair” MI400 GPUs and its “Venice” Epyc 9006 processors. Intel does not have an HPC-focused GPU in the market (although it does have ones aimed at inference), but there are also probably some customers who have acquired future “Diamond Rapids” Xeon 7 CPU with 256 P-cores, which will be about a year late to market if it debuts in the second half of 2027 using Intel’s 18A-P process (1.8 nanometers) as the rumor mill is suggesting. Intel said on its call with Wall Street analysts going over its third quarter financial results (when I was having major surgery, so I missed it) that the Diamond Rapids chip with 16 memory channels is sampling now. The mainstream Diamond Rapids with only eight memory channels has been killed off and the existing “Granite Rapids” Xeon 6+ will fill in the gap until Intel does a Xeon 8 refresh sometime in the future.

“The result does not indicate that performance has stopped growing,” write the caretakers of the Top500 list. (That would be Erich Strohmaier, of the Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, Jack Dongarra, of the University of Tennessee and Oak Ridge National Lab, and Horst Simon, of the ADIA Lab in Abu Dhabi.) “Instead, it shows that a larger share of improvement is coming from additions and upgrades below the very top rather than from wholesale replacement of leading installations.”

All that said, I still believe the stall is more about roadmap timing – particularly with networking, which is stalled at 800 Gb/sec ports when the world is expecting 1.6 Tb/sec ports – than it is moving workloads to the cloud at the same time there are much better compute engines ramping next year.

We will see as the June 2027, November 2027, and June 2028 Top500 supercomputer rankings come out. To balance things out, I would expect about two dozen extra machines to be installed to cover the drop experienced in the November 2026 rankings. If the June 2027 list is a little light, then the following two lists will have to be above average for things to balance out.

The thing to also remember whenever you look at the Top500 rankings is that the list is comprised of machines that have submitted HPL benchmark results formally for bragging rights. It is not intended to be an exhaustive list of all of the HPC systems that are installed in the world. Many organizations with fairly large or truly monstrous machines that are doing HPC work on them do not submit results; and many smaller organizations do submit results. The result is that we get a skewed view of the HPC systems market. Moreover, it is not a complete list even of those machines that have been tested running HPL and that are still in use. There are always only 500 unique machines on the list, even if there are probably somewhere on the order of 3,000 proper HPC sites worldwide, many with multiple machines – and I am not including AI training and inference systems in that number. I mean machines that do ModSim as their day job, which is only what should count and which is my major gripe about the middle and end of the Top500 list. There are a lot of clusters from clouds and telecom providers and software companies that most certainly do not do HPC as their day job.

All that said, the Top500 list is one of the few ways we get to see different architectural choices that HPC centers are making over time. And as such, I think this is still very valuable.

There are only 27 new machines that were added in the November 2026 Top500 list, which also means only 27 less powerful machines were knocked off the list. This is the lowest amount of churn across the 68 Top500 lists that have been compiled since 1993.

Six lists ago, I decided to focus in on the new machines in each Top500 ranking and try to organize them by architecture to get a better sense of what HPC people are buying and installing as time goes by. I think this is a much better use of this list than just looking at the list as a whole, which has some truly old machinery on it at any given time. I think a rolling list with machines that are not older than four years or maybe five years – probably five given that HPC centers are stretching how long machines are in the field, just like the hyperscalers and cloud builders are – might be a better indicator of what is going on out there in HPC Land, and sometime next year I will start doing such a sort. (If I get some extra time, I can back cast it into the 2022 and 2023 Top500 lists and do it sooner.) The point is, the fact that a very large machine that was very expensive and is very old is still in use is interesting, of course, but it doesn’t tell you what new things people are choosing. I love that we use these machines for a long time, but when this machines hang around on the official Top500 list, that means another newer machine that might make the list can’t.

Here is how the number of new machines added to the past six Top500 rankings, which comprises 264 machines from June 2024 through November 2026. The table below shows the number of cores across those machines, the Rmax throughput on the HPL test, and the Rpeak peak theoretical performance inherent in the system. Take a gander:

You will note, no doubt, that the number of cores – which is actually CPU cores and GPU streaming multiprocessors (SMs) added up across the compute engines in the machines – across those 27 new machines is quite large, at 71.4 million cores. But it gets weirder.

There is a China Telecom cloud in Shanghai called the eSurfing Cloud that has an infrastructure as a service (IaaS) offering based on China’s 56-core Hygon C86 X86-based server CPU, which is itself derived from a Zen1 core licensed many years ago from AMD, as well as the C588 GPU from Chinese chip maker MetaX. That machine has 66.63 million cores and SMs across its compute complexes, which are built from nodes with two CPUs and eight GPUs. None of them is particularly powerful compared to what is available in the United States, however, and this cloud cluster only had 38.66 petaflops of peak performance and only rated 18.36 petaflops sustained on the HPL benchmark. This one “machine” on the cloud represented 93.3 percent of all of the cores across the 27 new machines on the November 2026 list, but only represented 2.9 percent of the Rpeak performance aggregated across those 27 machines.

You can see the feeds and speeds of those new “HPC” machines in the table below:

The most powerful new machine on the list is the “Hangang” system at the KISTI supercomputing center in South Korea, which is based on Nvidia Grace-Hopper superchips and is made by Hewlett Packard Enterprise Cray EX254n server nodes and using HPE’s Slingshot 400 interconnect. The Hangang machine has a peak performance of 588.3 petaflops, and was one of five Grace-Hopper or Grace-Blackwell systems across the newbie systems, which as a group comprised 51.8 percent of all new capacity. (682.5 petaflops of aggregate compute.)

The second largest new machine in the November 2026 Top500 is the “Lux” supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which is made from HPE ProLiant XD685 nodes and uses a combination of “Turin” Epyc 9575F CPUs and “Antares” MI355X GPU accelerators. This machine is rated at 323.9 petaflops.

The rest of the machines are miniscule by comparison, and if you add them all up, Rpeak is only 1.32 exaflops aggregate across all of them.

One of the other things I like to do with the Top500 twice a year is look at how accelerated machines are being used as opposed to CPU-only machines. In some cases, the CPU is actually augmented with a huge amount of vector and sometimes matrix math, so it is not strictly speaking much like a general purpose CPU (think of the A64FX processor used in the “Fugaku” system at RIKEN Lab in Japan, for instance.)

This time around, there are 290 machines that have GPU or other kinds of accelerators to goose their floating point performance out of the 500 on the list:

The accelerated systems comprise 58 percent of machines, but 70.4 percent of total cores on the list and 79.9 percent of total peak exaflops. To be precise, the accelerated machines have an aggregate of 22,64 exaflops of FP64 oomph, compared to 5.7 exaflops of CPU-only peak theoretical performance. Nvidia has the lion’s share of the machines, but AMD GPUs are in a lot of very large machines and has 37.7 percent of FP64 flops compared to 52.9 percent for machines using Nvidia GPUs.

It will be interesting to see how AMD’s MI430X, which is aimed explicitly at the HPC crowd and which has very high real FP64 performance, does in the coming year and a half as shipments of this accelerator ramp and take on Nvidia GPUs with emulated, software-based FP64 computing atop matrix math engines instead of true FP64 performance.

item.title: Cerebras Readies CS-5 Systems For 2027 Launch As It Bags Another Hyperscaler
item.description:
Upstart waferscale AI compute maker Cerebras Systems has been very upfront for all of 2026 that this was a year to build out its cloud and to ramp up its manufacturing capability so it can start meeting the demands of the contracts it has inked with OpenAI and now Amazon Web Services, Oracle Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Thus far, most of its revenue backlog and all of its incremental revenue is coming from that OpenAI deal, which is finally ramping.

Next year is going to be a banner year for many AI system providers, and there is a non-zero chance that this could be the peak spending year for the GenAI boom. We shall see, and even AI systems do a terrible job at predicting the future. All anyone knows is what their customers tell them, and all those organizations know is what their customers tell them, and so on down and up the chain of being. Bullshit sometimes begets even bigger bullshit, but sometimes it isn’t bullshit and people really do buy a ton of systems. Which has happened for the past four years now despite the fears that the gravy train might run out of coal.

Here is the thing, though: This GenAI thing is real. It is just a matter of time, driven by ever-decreasing cost of token chewing and spitting, before it becomes pervasive in the world’s applications, or around the world’s applications. Some go too far and think as the world’s applications, and that is because they do not understand the nature of risk avoidance by the millions of corporations around the world. There is mainframe code older than me at the center of our banking and insurance systems, and wave after wave of technological evolution since I entered the IT sector four decades ago has augmented that code but a very large portion of it is still there, like a granite mountain.

In the third quarter, Cerebras didn’t sell as much of its CS-3 and CS-4 hardware as it has done in prior quarters, and that stands to reason because the company was building out its cloud services business in support of the $10 billion inference deal that the company inked with AI model builder OpenAI back in January 2026.

Since then, that deal, for 750 megawatts of gear that OpenAI can rent for fast inference, has been expressed as being worth $20 billion and sometimes $30 billion between 2026 and 2032, inclusive. That larger revenue stream is apparently possible if OpenAI has Cerebras build an additional 1.25 gigawatts of capacity by the end of 2030 and the contract for services runs out to 2032. Provided OpenAI goes public and has the cash, there is no reason to believe that it will not stretch this deal to the max. This option by definition has to be cheaper than buying Nvidia GPUs for inference prefill and Nvidia Grok LPUs for decode. Particularly with Cerebras using AMD GPUs for prefill, as it is doing in its cloud.

In the third quarter, hardware sales at Cerebras were down 28.8 percent to $68.9 million, and because the Cerebras factory is still ramping to a new production level gross margins were pretty bad at only 11 percent of revenues instead of the long-term goal of 60 percent. Andrew Feldman, co-founder and chief executive officer at the company, told Wall Street analysts in a conference call that margins in Q3 2026 were also adversely affected by the aggressive pricing that an early customer – presumably cloud provider G42 – negotiated years ago for machines being installed now.

The has been some jawboning out there on the intertubes that Cerebras has a yield problem, and Feldman brought the boot down on that idea. And it stands to reason. The WSE-3 used in the CS-3 systems and the WSE-3 Turbo used in the CS-4 systems are based on very mature 5 nanometer processes from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co – nothing crazy like the 2 nanometer processes that AMD is spearheading with its “Venice” Epyc 9006 server CPUs, just launched this week. The WSE-3 Turbo is a stop-gap, double-clocked waferscale processor that Cerebras put into the market in August in the CS-4 systems and there is a WSE-5 (you can’t have a WSE-4 because there isn’t going to be one) in the works for next summer for the CS-5 machines. These CS-4 and CS-5 systems will compete with new GPUs from Nvidia and AMD and LPUs and other XPUs from Grok (essentially owned by Nvidia), SambaNova, Rebellions, and the homegrown gear from the hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders themselves.

“Our product road map continues to advance rapidly,” Feldman explained on the call. “Our CS-4 will soon be in full production, doubling both performance and throughput. Our next-generation processor, the Wafer Scale Engine 5, which will be deployed in our fifth-generation CS-5 system, is back from the fab ahead of schedule. The WSE-5 taped out on June 15. The chip is back, has been brought up, and is already running models and is undergoing in-chassis testing. Moving from tape-out to system test in less than five months is exceptional execution. The CS-5 will more than double the speed of CS-4. It will enter production in early summer of 2027. It is built on TSMC's 5 nanometer node, where competition for wafers is less intense and wafer costs are much lower.”

It is safe to say that that WSE-5 has been in development for a long time, and I strongly suspect that as technology has advanced, it has been tweaked to incorporate new things. I think there are all kinds of technological possibilities for this WSE-5 engine, including silicon photonics optical connections linking wafers and memory servers and SRAM stacking – two that I favor for the sake of Cerebras. At Hot Chips this past summer, Cerebras revealed that it would be using 3D stacked DRAM with its wafers.

I also think that given the need for fast inference, the wafers will be double-clocked from this point forward. Performance trumps power consumption and heat dissipation these days – dollars per millions of tokens is what matters more than dollars per millions of tokens per watt at this stage of GenAI commercialization. Electricity is cheaper than the systems, even if it is getting harder and harder to come by. Cerebras can always offer two different clock speeds at the same price and let customers decide.

We shall see next summer. . . .

Given the lumpiness of hardware sales at all supercomputer makers – and make no mistake, the CS family is comprised of supercomputers – it is best to look at the company’s financials on an annual, not quarterly basis. Here is how 2022 through 2025 and projections for GAPP revenue (mine), not the non-GAAP revenue (which is larger) that Cerebras talks about in its financial presentations for Q3 and Q4:

And for those of you who like the raw numbers, here are the quarterly and annual results in the typical TPM monster table:

My best guess is that on a GAAP basis, Cerebras will close 2026 with around $885 million in revenues, up 73.4 percent compared to 2025’s sales. Operating income and net income were whacked by a spike in research and development spending and stock-based compensation. Feldman said on the Wall Street call that the company expected to triple its sales in 2027, and it is reasonable to assume that as manufacturing ramps and Cerebras increases its margins on hardware with partners Flex and Sanmina that gross profits and operating income will be much improved in 2027.

Cerebras ended the third quarter with $7.36 billion in cash and equivalents in the bank and a revenue backlog of $26.1 billion, mostly from the OpenAI deal. The AWS, Oracle, and Microsoft deals are not yet in the backlog and are certainly not yet bringing in revenue. Cerebras has been pretty vague about what these deals are, but it is important to note that three of the biggest clouds in the world are going to be working CS iron into their inference workloads, presumably for decode operations. Whatever WSE-5 and the resulting CS-5 system is, this is what they almost certainly want, especially given that WSE-5 will have 2X the performance of the WSE-3 Turbo compute engine that is available now.

item.title: The Nvidia Machine Is Self-Sustaining – And Was Already Facing A Tougher Future
item.description:
Well, like most of you on Earth, I didn’t see that coming.

The third and most important of the co-founders of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has resigned as president and chief executive officer and Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer of the company, has been tapped as his interim replacement in the wake of the revelation of two affairs by Huang – one with an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed International (who may be a Chinese government operative) and another with an executive in the top ranks at Nvidia itself.

There is a lot of chatter that Megaspeed was channeling either Nvidia-based GPU systems or remote access to them (or both) to Chinese companies, including upstart model maker DeepSeek, and it is not clear if Huang knew this when a sister company of Megaspeed bought $4.8 billion in Nvidia GPU gear between June 2024 and February 2026. The Information is reporting that Megaspeed and its affiliates have acquired $7.5 billion in GPU systems since 2023. The US Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, according to the timeline put together by the New York Times , but those investigations apparently stalled as President Trump and Jensen Huang started getting chummy last year. The investigations were moved over to the US Department of Justice, and it is unclear what state they are in.

Suffice it to say, the new Congress being sworn in coming January 2027 will be all over this issue, and eventually facts will be gathered and punishments will be meted out as appropriate – and a presidential pardon for Jensen Huang should he be indicted for being complicit in the smuggling of systems made by Inspur into China or the renting of capacity on systems to Megaspeed customers like Alibaba.

It is not clear that the latter is yet illegal, but if you are putting export controls on physical machines, it only makes sense that you should have export controls on selling capacity from a cloud over the wires. In any event, Alibaba obviously builds its own AI models and would benefit from having access to Nvidia GPUs that are under export controls and are forbidden to be sold to organizations in China. It is also not clear where Megaspeed got its money to buy GOU systems and to build datacenters in Indonesia and China, but it is reasonable to infer that it stretches back into China.

Let the chips fall where they may.

For now, Harvey Jones, who was once chief executive officer at chip design software maker Synopsis and who is a managing partner with venture capitalist Square Wave Ventures, has been tapped as chairman of the board. This is the first time Nvidia has had a chairman. Jones has been on the board of Nvidia since November 1993, shortly after the company was founded in April 1993. The board is starting a CEO search to replace Huang and Kress, and there is every reason to believe that Kress will continue in her role as CFO in the wake of the new CEO coming in.

Aside from all of these issues, the biggest one is how the AI industry and Nvidia within it will work without Jensen Huang in the middle of it, being the ambassador for the AI future as well as its biggest beneficiary of the GenAI revolution that no company has capitalized on better than Nvidia. (That revolution has made Huang the 15 th richest person in the world, with $145 billion of Nvidia stock ahead of the affair revelations earlier this week.) Huang has to give up $108 million in share compensation by stepping down, and his 3.6 percent stake in Nvidia is also taking some lumps, but he will have plenty of capital to start something new if he so desires to do so. It seems likely that Huang will try to lay low for a while, and try to heal his relationships with his wife and children. The world will likely not let him lay low.

As for Nvidia, Huang is famous for running a tight ship and for having the company’s 60 top executive directly report to him so he knew exactly what everyone was doing and why. The good news for Nvidia is that this process is in place, and each of these five dozen executives are well acquainted with their jobs. Moreover, the Nvidia AI system roadmaps are set for the “Rubin” and “Feynman” generations of GPUs that will carry the company into 2030, and Nvidia’s production is sold out for 2027 already and it won’t be long before it is sold out for 2028 if history and increasing demand is any guide. If there was a time where Nvidia can largely run itself, it is now.

That said, Nvidia has never faced so many pressures from so many different forces at the same time.

The hyperscalers, cloud builders, and AI model builders are all working on their own custom CPUs and XPU AI accelerators to not only wean themselves off of very expensive Nvidia iron and to create hardware specifically to run their own AI models for around half of what it costs to do it with the Nvidia hardware and systems software stack.

Moreover, Nvidia is championing open source and open weight AI models – something only Nvidia can afford to do because it gets such a high premium for its AI compute and networking hardware. These open Nemotron models directly compete against the closed source and usually closed weight models of its largest GPU accelerator customers, which probably has them irked a bit.

But even more alarming for those who have enjoyed the meteoric rise of Nvidia during the GenAI boom, it is not clear that the rosy forecasts for AI spending out in 2029 and 2030 and beyond can be met because of supply chain constraints for many components as well as the difficulty of adding more electricity capacity to the grids of the world.

And in America at least, there is rising dissatisfaction for what is perceived of as preferential treatment that datacenter operators have enjoyed for the past decade and a half. It is not a coincidence that residential electric bills have gone up as datacenters have proliferated, and people are annoyed by the elitist attitudes of the tech titans who control AI. They are also rightly concerned with what GenAI will do to the economies, societies, and cultures of the world.

Finally, by Huang exiting the top job at Nvidia, the AI industry just got a lot less coherent and eloquent. And now we will find out just how important Huang would have been in a future that was already much less certain for Nvidia before he was compelled to leave the company.

item.title: CoreWeave Is Accelerating To Escape Velocity Thanks To GPU Shortages
item.description:
CoreWeave, arguably the king of the neoclouds that focus exclusively on AI processing as opposed to the full breadth of compute in the datacenter, has had its share of doubters and critics. And the consequent whipsawing around of its share price and people go bull or bear on it.

But thanks to the undersupply of GPUs in the world and the extreme desire to use them to train AI models and to run inference workloads against them, pricing for the vintage GPUs in the CoreWeave fleet are going up and up and up, and that means the company’s revenues are also rising and, not at all coincidentally but quite deliberately, so is CoreWeave’s operating profits. Which is all well and good. But the heavy debt load that CoreWeave has – roughly $48 billion by our math – is very expensive to service.

But here is the thing. That debt is being used to fund capital expenses that expand the CoreWeave datacenter footprint and its AI server fleet, and the quicker it builds out this fleet, the quicker it can start booking revenue against it. Companies are prepaying billions of dollars for capacity ahead of time, which is now being used to fund capex as well, and an even larger increase in demand for GPUs or a crimping of supply would only help CoreWeave make more money sooner.

In short, the economics of the GenAI boom are starting to play in CoreWeave’s favor, which company co-founder and chief executive officer Michael Intrator explained as part of his going over the company’s financial results for the third quarter of 2026.

“In July, we increased pricing across SKUs by approximately 25 percent, followed by another 10 percent increase later in the quarter,” Intrator explained. “Pricing has continued to move higher in Q4, more than offsetting cost increases. We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four- and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt. Long-term commitments provide the visibility that supports our build-out. Short-term contracts let us respond to a strong pricing environment and earn premium returns. We weigh that trade-off contract by contract, assessing the full economics of an investment, the revenue it can earn, the cost of operating it, and the cost of financing it. Strong demand gives us choices in how we best create durable value.”

To make his point, Intrator added that rental prices for Nvidia “Ampere” A100 GPUs in the CoreWeave fleet rose by 30 percent sequentially in the third quarter, and rental prices for “Hopper” H100 and H200 GPUs rose by 50 percent sequentially. That’s pretty damned good for the A100s, which are six and a half years old (they started shipping in May 2020), and the H100s, which are four years old (they started shipping in September 2022). The A100s have been written down completely is my guess and the H100s are probably going to be written down entirely next year. This means selling their capacity is very profitable even after taking out operating costs for the systems that use these vintage GPUs.

To further make his point, Intrator said that 130,000 GPUs would come off contract and be open for new deals at higher prices, and another 170,000 GPUs would be up for renewal in 2028. (My guess is that CoreWeave has around 1.25 million GPUs installed right now, based on its active power, just to give you a sense of how small a part of the fleet the renewals in 2027 and 2028 represent.) Intrator did a little math and said that the 2027 renewals would generate $4 billion in incremental annualized revenues at the current (and higher) prices and this would grow to an incremental $10 billion annualized revenues for the 2028 renewals.

“If datacenter construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute becomes scarcer and the knock-on effect is that GPU pricing may stay higher for longer,” Intrator explained. “In that scenario, being first matters. Our installed base comes off contract, fully paid, years ahead of most others in the market. We're well positioned across a range of market conditions. If the industry builds quickly, we grow with it. If supply is delayed, our installed paid-off fleet becomes more valuable. We do not build our plan on that scenario. The plan rests on contracted demand, success-based capex and the contracts we are already signing.”

All of this is why the chart below makes sense:

There is a direct correlation to the size of the CoreWeave GPU fleet, which I have estimated based on the active power each quarter, and the revenue backlog that CoreWeave is able to build. The correlation is very strong, as you can see. And it makes perfect sense.

But like a shark, the business has to keep moving to keep building that backlog, and at some point the debt load has to stop growing faster than revenues. That has to happen before the GenAI bubble bursts. I still believe that it will be very hard to find the power for the buildout that is expected in the IT sector in 2029 and 2030. We seem to be relatively safe in 2027 and into 2028, given so much of the capacity purchased is prepaid.

In the third quarter ended in September, CoreWeave booked $3.66 billion in sales, up 2.7X year on year and up 42.2 percent sequentially from the second quarter. Operating income was actually a positive $207 million, compared to an operating income of $52 million a year ago. But because of the debt service, the company’s net loss expanded by a factor of 6.4X to $709 million. Hence, losses are outpacing revenue growth. Not taking on more debt and using the proceeds from price increases to fund capex expansion – which is indeed the plan – will help get things back into whack. Or more precisely, into whack for the first time in CoreWeave’s history.

We shall see. But, the price increases and the demand to support them are encouraging signs.

If you like to drill down into the numbers yourself, here are the trends since Q1 2024:

CoreWeave exited the quarter with just under $5.6 billion in cash and equivalents and shelled out $14.5 billion for capital expenses. For the year so far, CoreWeave has spent $30.7 billion on datacenter gear and facilities. The company ended the quarter with a revenue backlog of $132.5 billion, up 2.4X year on year.

item.title: How The “Venice” Epycs Measure Up Against Prior AMD Server CPUs
item.description:
Over the past decade, each generation of Epyc processors from AMD is more complex and that complexity is leveraged not because the company’s top techies are baroque, but because it takes actual engineering distinctions to address the widening number and kind of workloads in the modern datacenter.

With the “Venice” generation of Epyc chips that launch today – the sixth generation and one that will once again put more water between itself and X86 CPU rival Intel – AMD is bringing to bear two different server sockets, two different I/O dies, and two different compute dies to create a product line that initially has 31 different CPUs initially, spanning from 8 cores to 256 cores, 130 watts to 600 watts, and from $700 to $14,904 when purchased in 1,000-unit trays from the company.

We have already discussed how AMD believes the Venice Epycs address today’s workload needs and also very generally how they compare to alternatives from X86 rival Intel and the Arm collective. This story walks through the Venice SKU stack and how the top bin and middle bin parts compare to the prior five generations of Epycs and the touchstone “Shanghai” quad-core Opteron processors were launched way back at the beginning of the Great Recession in November 2008.

The Salient Feeds And Speeds

Before we dive into the SKUs, we need to talk a little tech.

Rather than keep the Zen 6 and Zen 6c designs in distinct processor families within the Venice line, as AMD has done during the prior “Genoa” and “Turin” generations, the company has decided to blur the distinction between the Zen 6 and Zen 6 cores by keeping the cache hierarchies the same but in optimizing the schedulers inside the two cores in different ways – one optimized for higher core counts and lower clock speeds on the core compute dies (CCDs) and the other optimized for lower cores and higher clock speeds. With the prior Turin Zen 5c cores, AMD cut the L3 cache on each CCD in half and that allowed it to put more cores on the die but also crimped its performance on cache-sensitive workloads. This new approach seems sensible. Both the 12-core CCD, which has 48 MB of L3 cache, and the 32-core CCD, which has 128 MB of L3 cache, are etched using 2 nanometer processes from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

The other big change is that there are two different sockets, and both kinds of CCDs are used to make some of the CPU SKUs in both sockets.

The SP7 socket, which is shipping now and which makes heftier Venice processors, has a pair of I/O dies that deliver 16 channels of DDR5 memory that can deliver up to 1.6 TB/sec of bandwidth using MRDIMMs running at 12.8 GT/sec and 1 TB/sec using regular RDIMMs running at 8 GT/sec. Each channel can have one memory stick and they can be up to 512 GB in capacity. (If you think you can afford that. . . .) The SP7 socket has 96 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes running at 64 Gb/sec each with eight PCI-Express 4.0 lanes running at 16 Gb/sec; in a two socket configuration, 128 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes plus sixteen PCI-Express 4.0 lanes are exposed to the outside world and 64 of those PCI-Express lanes are used to make a NUMA link between a pair of CPU sockets.

This SP7 socket I/O (and memory) die is made using 6 nanometer processes from TSMC, just like the I/O (and memory) die for the Turin generation was, but this is clearly a different design. As we have pointed in the past, there is not a lot of benefit from using the most advanced processes to etch I/O and other signaling chiplets because I/O does not shrink as well as compute does. Such a shrink makes signaling more difficult and is also more expensive – two good reasons to hang back on the manufacturing process.

Here are the nine Venice chips that plug into the SP7 socket:

As we have done with past Epyc processors, we have calculated the relative performance of the Venice chips based on core count, clock speed, and improvement in instructions per clock (IPC) from generation to generation for integer workloads. This time around, the average performance uplift per core at the same clock speed for the Zen 6 core compared to the Zen 5 core, according to AMD, is 20 percent. This is a relatively big jump and is a testament to the core designers who are always coming up with new ways to get the core to do more work each cycle.

By the way, the Epyc 9G76 processor highlighted in blue font and red background in the SP7 socket processor table above is the one AMD has made specifically for the Helion AI racks. It is not particularly different from the Epyc 9686F chip aimed at HPC workloads, but I think they are distinct so they can be discounted differently. The hyperscalers and cloud builders are no doubt going to get better deals than the HPC centers of the world, given the high volumes they are purchasing.

Moving on to the SP8 socket, which is used for more mainstream Venice Epyc processors. And as such, it has only eight DDR5 memory channels per socket (four per I/O die) with two DIMMs per channel interleaving to boost capacity. The I/O die for the SP8 socket has 128 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes and eight bonus PCI-Express 4.0 lanes. So, half the memory bandwidth but 33 percent more I/O. In a two-socket NUMA setup, 64 PCI-Express 6.0 lanes are used to make the NUMA coherency and 192 lanes are exposed to the outside world plus those sixteen PCI-Express 4.0 bonus lanes. (That is for the pair of I/O dies, of course.)

AMD has confirmed to us that the SP8 I/O (and memory) die is etched with TSMC 6 nanometer processes, as we expected.

Here are the 22 variants of the Venice Epyc CPUs outfitted for the SP8 socket:

The SP8 socket versions of the Venice CPUs will not ship until next year, and it is my guess that it will happen fairly early in the year although officially all that AMD is saying is that they will ship sometime in the first half of 2027.

Comparisons Are Absolutely Not Odious

With that out of the way, lets see how the top bin parts and middle bin parts across the history of the Epyc line stack up in terms of performance and price/performance, and as usual we are using that Shanghai Opteron line as the baseline against which all comparisons are made. These were pretty much the last competitive Opterons that AMD shipped, which came out in the wake of the “Nehalem” Xeon 5500 chips where Intel copied an awful lot off of AMD’s homework and finally got a decent multicore chip out the door just as the Great Recession was starting and AMD was having issues with the Opterons.

Bad timing for AMD, good timing for Intel. But that is all ancient history now, and this time around AMD is not leaving any crack to exploit as AMD just keeps making better and better server CPUs and eats a little more market share with every passing quarter. It is a wonder that Intel has been able to hold onto the market share is does get, to be honest.

Let’s start with the top bin parts:

In these comparisons, I ignored the special HPC variants that AMD has shipped from time to time, which are denoted with a F designation for frequency optimized and an X designation of they have extra vertical cache on the package. So these are top bin standard parts.

Also, I put top bin parts in the comparison for both the SP7 and SP8 variants in the Venice lineup.

As is immediately obvious in the chart above, the relative performance of the top bin Epycs have scaled linearly, more or less, from the “Naples” Epyc 7001 series all the way through the Venice 9006 series with the SP8 socket. The SP7 socket with 256 cores is a total outlier in terms of the performance boost, and it takes the throughout performance up an exponential scale as you can see with your own eyes.

What also pops out instantly is how the bang for the buck of the first generation Naples processors improved compared to those Shanghai Opterons, but you have to remember that the gap in time is nine years – nine IT years where Moore’s Law was still available to boost performance and improve economics. (The Shanghai Opterons were etched in TSMC 45 nanometer processes, the Naples chips used GlobalFoundries 14 nanometer processes.)

What you can also see is how aggressively AMD moved in terms of price/performance with the “Rome” second generation Epycs, which is when the company first moved to distinct compute tiles and an I/O die linking them together and to the outside world. With the Milan Epycs, performance went up for the top bin part, but value for dollar improvement slowed and the same thing happened again with the fourth-gen “Genoa” top bin parts. But with the Turin and Now Venice parts, AMD is once again pushing the price/performance envelope, and it is particularly awarding customers who go with the throughput-oriented SP7 variants. AMD is charging a slight premium for the SP8 versions of Venice, which have half as many cores that run a little bit faster.

Clock speed is always going to come at a premium because that adds heat faster than increasing cores after a process shrink.

The net result is that the Epyc 9996 SP7 part has 190X more oomph than the Opteron 2393 SE, and if offers that performance at a cost per unit of performance that is 14.9X lower. For AMD, the benefit is that the chip costs 12.8X as much and companies are happy to pay for it for server consolidation and agentic AI and traditional HPC workloads. For the Venice Epyc 9746 SP8 chip, the performance jump compared to the Shanghai Opteron 2393 SE is 108.2X, the bang for the buck has improved by 10.8X, and the price per chip is 10X higher.

The curve for middle bin server CPUs from AMD looks similar if a little flatter in some ways:

But once again, the value for dollar with Venice is a lot better than it was compared across prior Epyc CPU generations.

AMD is not only keeping the heat on Intel. It is turning it up. And it has to if it is to compete against the Arm collective that is rising among the hyperscalers and cloud builders who account for half of the server market these days.

item.title: AMD Tunes Up CPUs For Agentic AI With “Venice” Epyc Processors
item.description:
The introduction of the ChatGPT chatbot by OpenAI in late 2022 supercharged the launch of of the GenAI era that shows only a few signs of slowing down, at least in the near term.

The Democratic “Blue Wave” in the recent midterm elections in the United States, which could introduce more regulation for the AI industry and become a drag on the datacenter building boom around the country, could tap the brakes, and the latest scandal involving Nvidia co-founder and chief executive officer Jensen Huang could be a blip on the screen or a longer-term issue. It’s hard to tell how this will shake out.

That said, the emerging agentic AI market is forecast to expand rapidly, with some analyst firms calling for it to grow almost 43 percent annually between now and 2034. Agentic AI also will drive a shift within datacenter infrastructure. Over the past four years, the various waves of generative AI like reasoning and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have been a boon for GPU makers – none more than Nvidia , which has seen its valuation soar into the trillions – and pushed the CPU, long the processor of choice for datacenter operators, into a supporting role.

But the computation demands of agentic AI are different from those of chattybot GenAI models froma few years back and require the capabilities that CPUs bring to the table for both AI host processors and AI sandboxes that run code generated by AI models.

In the agentic AI era, “the shape of the workload changes entirely,” Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager for compute and enterprise AI at AMD, wrote in May . “Instead of answering one prompt, an agent breaks a goal into steps, decides what to do next, calls multiple models, queries databases, connects with APIs, runs enterprise applications, checks permissions, retrieves memory, validates output and then loops back through the process again. It’s a very different infrastructure profile than prompt-in-answer-out chatbot AI.”

CPUs are better than GPUs at orchestrating the various complex AI agent tasks, as well as policy, security, and agent execution. That promises to change what’s needed in datacenter systems. Right now, the ratio of GPUs to CPUs is somewhere between 1:4 and 1:8. The expectation is that with agentic AI, that ratio will be brought to 1:1, more comfortable numbers for AMD, Intel, and other CPU makers.

That is a point AMD executives are making this week as the give more details about the 6 th Gen Epyc CPUs – formerly known as “Venice” – and the 6 th generation of the Zen microarchitecture. As Mike Clark, Corporate Fellow, senior vice president, and lead Zen architect at AMD, told journalists and analysts during recent briefing, “we didn't have a foresight that agentic was going to be what it has become, but we have always believed that the Core Complex Die was going to play a critical role in AI. We did a big investment in Zen 5 to do that, but with Zen 6, we continued to invest down that path and enhance our AI capability and it's paying off as agentic has taken off.”

As we’ve written before, agentic AI doesn’t mean that AMD will be able to chase down Nvidia in the still booming GPU market, but the company will continue to fair well against long-time CPU rival Intel – AMD’s share of the datacenter CPU market is about 46 percent – and most importantly, make a lot of money doing so.

The message from Madhu Rangarajan, corporate vice president for compute and enterprise AI products, during the call with journalists and analysts, was that the developments in the “Venice” sixth generation Epyc X86 CPUs that make them fit so well with the demands of agentic AI were a natural progression in the evolution of the server CPUs over the past eight years, since the introduction of the first generation “Naples” chips in 2018.

With the fourth generation “Genoa” CPUs in 2022, AMD began to expand its roadmap to serve multiple datacenter market segments, Rangarajan said.

“So with your Genoa and your Turin and your Bergamo and your Siena, you had your optimized design points going after different sub-segments of the market,” he said. “That's where we really started growing up to have a full portfolio of products here, and continued that.”

Rangarajan echoed Clark, saying he couldn’t claim that AMD purpose-built the Venice CPU family for agentic AI, but said the chips fit well with the needs of AI agents because they spend a broad set of workloads, adding that “we really now have a portfolio ready for the agentic AI era. We’ve got 1,000-plus instances, and what that allows customers to do is get a consistent offering, no matter how they want it to fly.”

With the Venice Epyc 9006 series chips, AMD is essentially doubling the throughput from one generation to the next, with the Venice chips delivering 1.9X the throughput of the prior “Turin” Epyc 9005 processors. The CPUs also measure up to throughput and per-core performance when compared to Nvidia’s Vera , Intel’s 6 th Gen Xeon 6980P , and Arm’s AGI processors.

Here’s the first comparison to Nvidia Vera:

And here is the comparison to Intel and Arm CPUs:

AMD is increasing the speed of the Venice chips, from 5.0 GHz with 64 cores with Turin to 5.3 GHz with 96 cores. Memory bandwidth jumps from 12 channels of DDR5 at 614 GB/sec to 16 channels at 1.6 TB/sec while I/O bandwidth doubles from PCI-Express Gen 5 to Gen 6, too.

Concurrent agents is an important measure these days, according to Rangarajan. AMD’s 6 th Gen 256-core chip at 400 watts offers 3.3 times the agents-per-watt that Nvidia’s Vera does, 1.8 times the agents-per-dollar compared with Intel’s 6 th Gen Xeons, and 1.5 times the agents per Helion AI Rack than fit in a Vera rack.

The Epyc 9006 chips also deliver better density and efficiency than Vera, according to AMD.

As AMD pushes its latest generation of CPUs into a hot agentic AI market, such numbers matter as the types of workloads expand, Rangarajan said.

“What agentic AI is doing is it's driving CPU demand across three networks vs. just general-purpose servers,” he said. “Agents like to do searches, in search clusters. Agents execute enterprise tools – CRM, ERP – we increasingly have agents doing EVM workloads. Your agents are accessing databases. All of this needs a broad CPU portfolio for these workloads.”
